body.html:
Antibiotics underpin modern medicine: surgery, preterm care, transplants, complicated deliveries and cancer treatment. An antibiotic kills or inhibits bacteria without harming the host (selective toxicity); it is natural (fungi, bacteria: Penicillium notatum makes penicillin G) or synthetic, acts over hours, diffuses into tissues and is active at very low concentrations (mg/L). Antiseptics and disinfectants (alcohols, iodine, chlorhexidine) act in minutes, non-selectively, only locally and at high concentrations (%). Proper use means the right dose at the site, the right route, enough duration and no misuse; misuse drives resistance.

Classification rests on four pillars: chemical structure (families), spectrum, target and mode of action (bactericidal vs bacteriostatic).

All bind penicillin-binding proteins and block peptidoglycan synthesis: bactericidal. Penicillin G/V: streptococci, Neisseria, Listeria, Treponema pallidum, most anaerobes; not staphylococci making penicillinase, not Gram-negative bacilli (outer membrane). Penicillin M (methicillin, oxacillin, cloxacillin): penicillinase-producing S. aureus, but not MRSA, whose altered PBP has low affinity. Penicillin A (ampicillin, amoxicillin): adds non-β-lactamase-producing Gram-negatives (H. influenzae, E. coli, Salmonella, Shigella), not Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Serratia or Pseudomonas. Carboxy- and ureidopenicillins (ticarcillin, piperacillin) cover Pseudomonas. β-lactamase inhibitors (clavulanic acid, sulbactam, tazobactam, avibactam) have no antibacterial activity themselves; they are 'suicide inhibitors' protecting the partner β-lactam.

Cephalosporins: 1st generation (cefazolin) Gram-positives; 2nd (cefuroxime, cefoxitin) more Gram-negatives and some anaerobes; 3rd (cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, ceftazidime) very active on Gram-negative bacilli, diffusible, but inactive on enterococci and Listeria and destroyed by ESBLs; 4th (cefepime) adds Pseudomonas, Enterobacter; 5th (ceftaroline) active against MRSA. Carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem, ertapenem): widest spectrum, stable to most β-lactamases including ESBLs; reserved for severe or multiresistant hospital infections. Monobactam (aztreonam): aerobic Gram-negatives only.

title: Other cell wall and membrane agents
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.html: Glycopeptides (vancomycin, teicoplanin): bactericidal, Gram-positives only, including methicillin-resistant staphylococci. Fosfomycin: a structurally unique agent blocking an early step of wall synthesis; used as a single dose (fosfomycin trometamol) for urinary infections. Polymyxins (polymyxin B, colistin): cationic peptides disrupting Gram-negative membranes; natural resistance in Proteus, Serratia, Providencia; poor tissue diffusion and nephrotoxic, so kept for multiresistant Gram-negatives.

title: Protein and nucleic acid synthesis inhibitors
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.html:
Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin, tobramycin, streptomycin): bind 30S, cause misreading, bactericidal; given parenterally; active on aerobic Gram-negative bacilli, staphylococci and mycobacteria; inactive alone on streptococci and anaerobes; nephrotoxic and ototoxic. Macrolides, lincosamides and streptogramins (erythromycin, azithromycin, clarithromycin, clindamycin, pristinamycin): 50S, bacteriostatic; Gram-positives and intracellular or atypical bacteria (Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Legionella, Campylobacter). Tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline): 30S, bacteriostatic; intracellular bacteria (Brucella, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Rickettsia). Chloramphenicol: 50S, broad spectrum, excellent diffusion, but bone marrow aplasia; topical eye use, sometimes typhoid or meningitis.

Quinolones: nalidixic acid (Gram-negatives, urinary use); fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, ofloxacin) inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, broader spectrum including staphylococci and P. aeruginosa, excellent tissue and intracellular diffusion. Rifampicin inhibits RNA polymerase; key anti-tuberculosis drug, never used alone (selects resistant mutants). Metronidazole damages DNA of anaerobes. Sulfonamides + trimethoprim inhibit folate synthesis in sequence. Fusidic acid blocks elongation factor G.

Note: one slide places chloramphenicol on the 30S subunit; it binds the 50S subunit, as the lecture's summary table states.

Combinations treat mixed infections, broaden cover and prevent resistance ('if one fails, the second kills'). Synergy: ampicillin + gentamicin (enterococcal endocarditis), vancomycin + gentamicin (serious MRSA), trimethoprim + sulfamethoxazole, piperacillin-tazobactam + aminoglycoside (Pseudomonas). Antagonism: a bacteriostatic drug with a bactericidal β-lactam (penicillin + tetracycline or chloramphenicol in pneumococcal infection), because β-lactams need growing bacteria.

To act, a drug must cross the envelope, avoid efflux, stay active and reach its target; resistance attacks each step: enzymatic inactivation (β-lactamases, ESBLs, carbapenemases), target modification (altered PBP in MRSA), reduced permeability (porin loss) and efflux pumps. Wrong drugs or doses, use in viral infections and over-the-counter sales drive resistance. New agents include gepotidacin (a new topoisomerase inhibitor approved in 2025 for gonorrhoea).

Bordetella pertussis (Betaproteobacteria, family Alcaligenaceae) causes whooping cough. Related species: B. parapertussis (milder, human), B. bronchiseptica (animals, rarely zoonotic), B. avium (birds). B. pertussis is a strictly human, highly contagious pathogen spread by droplets, colonising the ciliated epithelium of the nasopharynx, trachea and bronchi.

It is a small Gram-negative coccobacillus (0.2-0.5 × 0.5-2 µm), single or in pairs, no true capsule, non-motile, strictly aerobic, oxidase and catalase positive, asaccharolytic, and fastidious: it needs charcoal- or blood-based media and forms pinpoint colonies after 3-6 days or more.

Adhesins: filamentous haemagglutinin (FHA), fimbriae (FIM2, FIM3), pertactin and tracheal colonisation factor. Toxins: pertussis toxin (PT), a protein exotoxin (causes lymphocytosis, raises insulin secretion, blunts immune cells), tracheal cytotoxin (ciliostasis and death of ciliated cells), adenylate cyclase toxin (paralyses phagocytes), dermonecrotic toxin and LPS/LOS endotoxin. The bacteria bind ciliated cells, paralyse cilia so mucus is not cleared, damage the lining and suppress innate and adaptive immunity, allowing persistence.

1. Catarrhal (1-2 weeks): coryza, low fever, mild cough; most contagious and hard to tell from a cold. 2. Paroxysmal (2-6 weeks or longer): bursts of rapid coughing from thick mucus, an inspiratory whoop, post-tussive vomiting, exhaustion, up to about 15 attacks a day, worse at night; apnoea in infants, who are at greatest risk. 3. Convalescent (weeks to months): cough gradually fades. A marked lymphocytosis, especially in children, is a useful clue.

Specimen: posterior nasopharyngeal swab (Dacron or flocked) or aspirate, not the anterior nostril, placed at once in transport medium (Amies with charcoal, Regan-Lowe). PCR is first line: faster, more sensitive (especially early) and positive after antibiotics; targets IS481 (sensitive but not fully specific) and the pertussis toxin promoter (ptxP) (more specific). Culture is the gold standard but insensitive: Regan-Lowe agar (charcoal, horse blood, cephalexin; reference medium) or Bordet-Gengou (potato, glycerol, blood), 35-37 °C, humid, no CO₂, 7-10 days; small shiny 'mercury drop' colonies. Confirmation by MALDI-TOF or 16S rRNA sequencing. Microscopy and biochemical tests are of little use. Serology (ELISA IgG/IgA against PT) is only retrospective and hard to interpret within a year of vaccination.

Macrolides are first line: azithromycin, erythromycin or clarithromycin; they are most effective early and reduce transmission even when the cough persists. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the alternative (intolerance, or suspected macrolide resistance, which is rare and not a major issue in Morocco). Failures are usually due to late treatment. Household contacts receive macrolide prophylaxis (erythromycin 14 days in the lecture).

Vaccination in Morocco: a whole-cell pertussis vaccine combined as DTP, usually the pentavalent DTP-HepB-Hib, at 2, 3 and 4 months, with boosters at 18 months and 5 years. Acellular multicomponent vaccines (PT, FHA, pertactin, fimbriae) are used in hexavalent and other combinations.

Chlamydia pneumoniae is an obligate intracellular bacterium, a strict human respiratory pathogen with no animal reservoir, spread by droplets. The lecture ranks it the third cause of community-acquired pneumonia after S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae. Infection is often asymptomatic or mild and can persist; it is associated with chronic respiratory disease and, controversially, atherosclerosis.

It has a Gram-negative-like envelope but lacks classical peptidoglycan, is non-motile, and depends on the host for ATP ('energy parasite'): it grows only inside cells, in membrane-bound inclusions, so it is extremely difficult to culture. Its biphasic cycle: the elementary body (EB, 0.2-0.3 µm) is infectious and metabolically inactive; the reticulate body (RB, 0.8-1 µm) is non-infectious and replicates.

Targets: non-ciliated respiratory epithelial cells and macrophages (which carry it to other sites, including the vascular endothelium). Virulence factors: MOMP and other outer membrane proteins (attachment and entry), inclusion membrane proteins (Incs) maintaining the protected vacuole, secreted proteins via a type III secretion system that modulate host signalling, apoptosis and immunity, inhibition of phagolysosome fusion, LPS (weak endotoxin but immunogenic) and proteases. Stress (e.g. interferon-γ) produces aberrant bodies: persistent infection and chronic inflammation.

About 70-90% of infections are asymptomatic. Symptomatic disease: pharyngitis, sinusitis, bronchitis and atypical pneumonia (gradual onset, dry cough, few signs). Chronic associations: asthma exacerbations, COPD; systemic association with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

Specimens: nasopharyngeal swab (preferred), aspirates, throat swabs or washings, sputum, bronchial washings, lung tissue; viability is fairly stable at 4 °C. Direct: NAATs (PCR) targeting ompA, 16S rRNA or incA, the method of choice; direct fluorescent antibody staining of infected HEp-2 cells is rarely used. Indirect: micro-immunofluorescence (MIF) against MOMP, sensitive and species-specific (no cross-reaction with C. trachomatis or C. psittaci), but IgM appears only about 3 weeks after symptoms and IgG reaches diagnostic levels at 6-8 weeks, and past and current infection are hard to separate; complement fixation is historical; ELISA is partly automated.

First line: macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin). Alternatives: doxycycline or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) in severe cases. Treatment is longer than for typical pneumonia (more than 10-14 days); severe cases get IV antibiotics and oxygen. β-lactams are ineffective (intracellular, no classical peptidoglycan). Resistance is rare. There is no vaccine: prevention relies on respiratory hygiene, hand washing, avoiding close contact during acute illness, not sharing utensils, ventilation and early treatment.

A large, heterogeneous family of clinically important Gram-negative bacilli (27 genera and over 100 species of medical interest). Shared features: oxidase negative, nitrate reductase positive, glucose fermenters, facultative anaerobes, non-sporing, growing easily on ordinary media at 35-37 °C; motile with peritrichous flagella (E. coli, most Salmonella) or non-motile (Shigella, Klebsiella). Habitat: the gut of humans and animals, some in water, soil and sewage. Transmission: faecal-oral, food and water, zoonotic, vector-borne, or endogenous from the patient's own flora.

Obligate pathogens: Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, some E. coli strains. Opportunists: E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Serratia, Proteus, Providencia, Citrobacter. Identification uses biochemical profiles (lactose, indole, methyl red, Voges-Proskauer, citrate, H₂S, urease), antigens (O somatic, H flagellar, K capsular) and molecular methods. On MacConkey, E. coli is a pink lactose fermenter (metallic green sheen on EMB); Salmonella and Shigella are pale non-fermenters on Hektoen, XLD or SS agar, Salmonella with black H₂S centres.

Virulence factors across the family: adhesins (fimbriae, pili), toxins, invasion factors, a type III secretion system, capsules, biofilm, siderophores and resistance mechanisms (β-lactamases, efflux, target changes).

The commonest aerobic isolate of the colon; harmless strains make vitamin K and block pathogens. Its LPS has the O polysaccharide, a core and lipid A (endotoxin); over 700 serotypes are defined by O, K, F and H antigens (e.g. O157:H7).

Extra-intestinal disease: urinary tract infection (about 90% of UTIs, ascending from the gut flora, attaching by pili: urgency, burning, frequency, pelvic pain, haematuria); neonatal infections by K1-capsulated strains transmitted from the mother (about 80% of neonatal meningitis and 40% of neonatal septicaemia in the lecture; fever, apnoea, poor feeding, jaundice, seizures); intra-abdominal, bone, skin infections and septicaemia.

Intestinal pathotypes: ETEC (LT and ST enterotoxins, watery diarrhoea, no invasion), EPEC (infant gastroenteritis, no spread), EIEC (Shigella-like invasion of colonic cells: dysentery with blood and leucocytes), EHEC (Shiga toxins Stx1/Stx2: abundant bloody diarrhoea without leucocytes, systemic toxin effects, haemolytic uraemic syndrome), plus EAEC and DAEC.

Diagnosis is direct: samples depend on the site (urine for ECBU, blood, CSF, stool); Gram-negative bacilli; culture on MacConkey or CLED; biochemical identification; antibiotic susceptibility testing is essential. Typing for outbreaks: serotyping (O, H, K), biochemical profiles, resistance patterns and molecular methods (PCR, PFGE, MLST, whole-genome sequencing).

Treatment depends on site, severity and susceptibility. In Morocco resistance is high and rising, especially in UTIs, with frequent ESBL producers: fluoroquinolones and third-generation cephalosporins are less reliable empirically; fosfomycin or nitrofurantoin for uncomplicated cystitis; carbapenems (± an aminoglycoside) for severe ESBL infections; always guided by the antibiogram.

A capsulated, non-motile Gram-negative bacillus forming large mucoid colonies; a gut commensal, also in soil and water, and an indicator of faecal contamination; spread by direct contact and in hospitals. It causes pneumonia (dense lobar consolidation with a 'bulging fissure', necrosis), urinary infections, septicaemia in the immunocompromised and many nosocomial infections. Virulence: the polysaccharide capsule (over 70 types; non-capsulated strains are less virulent), LPS (sepsis), fimbriae, siderophores, biofilm and β-lactamases. Hypervirulent K. pneumoniae (hvKp) causes community-acquired liver abscesses with metastatic spread (eye, lung).

Diagnosis: culture of sputum, urine, blood or pus; Gram stain; biochemistry (catalase +, oxidase −, nitrate +); susceptibility testing; imaging for deep infections. Treatment: Klebsiella is naturally resistant to ampicillin (chromosomal penicillinase). Hospital strains: piperacillin-tazobactam or amikacin if susceptible; ESBL strains (frequent in Moroccan hospitals): carbapenems ± amikacin; carbapenem-resistant (CRKP): colistin, tigecycline, combinations under specialist guidance; hvKp: ceftriaxone or fluoroquinolone if susceptible. Prevention: hand hygiene, contact precautions and isolation for MDR carriers, limiting catheters and ventilators, ICU bundles, antibiotic stewardship, screening and environmental cleaning.

Salmonella are Gram-negative, non-capsulated (except the Vi antigen of Typhi) bacilli, mostly motile, non-sporing; glucose fermenting, H₂S positive, nitrate reductase positive, oxidase and urease negative, lactose negative; facultative anaerobes growing at 37-42 °C. On Hektoen, XLD, SS or bismuth sulphite agar they form colourless colonies with black H₂S centres. They live in the intestines of birds, reptiles and mammals.

Typhoidal (S. Typhi, Paratyphi): strictly human, faecal-oral, about 22 million cases a year worldwide, endemic and travel-related; about 1 in 20 infected people becomes an asymptomatic carrier. Non-typhoidal serovars: zoonotic, from undercooked eggs, poultry, meat, dairy or contaminated vegetables, causing gastroenteritis, usually self-limited.

Pathogenesis: resistance to stomach acid and bile, adhesion and invasion of intestinal cells via the type III secretion system, survival in macrophages, bacteraemia and spread to liver, spleen and bone marrow; the Vi capsule and LPS aid survival; chronic gallbladder carriers keep shedding bacteria. Symptoms appear 1-3 weeks after exposure: sustained high fever (39-40 °C), headache, abdominal pain, lethargy, anorexia, swollen abdomen, rash (rose spots), constipation or diarrhoea. Complications: intestinal bleeding and perforation; untreated, fever lasts weeks to months and mortality can reach 30%.

Diagnosis: blood culture in the first week (80-90% positive before antibiotics), then stool, urine, bile or clot cultures; biochemical identification; slide agglutination with antisera; serology (Widal test, ELISA) of limited value. Treatment: fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin), ceftriaxone or cefixime, or azithromycin, adapted to resistance; rehydration, rest, hospital care for severe cases. Vaccines: oral live attenuated Ty21a (4 capsules, from 6 years, booster every 5 years) and injectable Vi polysaccharide (1 dose, from 2 years, booster every 2-3 years). Prevention: safe water, cooked food, no ice or raw vegetables in endemic areas.

Note: a slide lists S. Typhi as indole positive; Salmonella are indole negative, and S. Typhi is also citrate negative and produces only a little H₂S.

Both are motile Gram-negative bacilli of the gut flora and the hospital environment (water, sinks, devices), late lactose fermenters, oxidase and indole negative. Enterobacter aerogenes has been renamed Klebsiella aerogenes for its genetic closeness to Klebsiella; it has a more prominent capsule, stronger biofilm and outbreak potential. Both are classic ICU opportunists: UTIs, pneumonia, bacteraemia and wound infections, spread by hands, catheters, ventilators and contaminated fluids.

Their key feature is a chromosomal AmpC β-lactamase: intrinsic resistance to ampicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate and first- and second-generation cephalosporins, with a risk of selecting AmpC-overproducing mutants under third-generation cephalosporins. Treatment is guided by susceptibility testing: cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam if susceptible, carbapenems for severe or ESBL infections, amikacin in combination, colistin or tigecycline for carbapenem-resistant strains. Prevention: hand hygiene, contact precautions, device limitation, aseptic technique, ICU bundles, environmental cleaning, stewardship and surveillance.

Proteus mirabilis, P. vulgaris and P. penneri are Gram-negative, non-capsulated bacilli (1-3 µm) with very high motility, producing a characteristic swarming film over blood agar; non-lactose fermenters on MacConkey; catalase and nitrate positive, oxidase negative, and strongly urease positive. P. mirabilis is indole negative, P. vulgaris indole positive. They are gut commensals causing endogenous and catheter-associated infections.

Virulence: urease splits urea to ammonia, making the urine alkaline and precipitating magnesium ammonium phosphate: struvite (infection) stones and catheter encrustation; flagella and swarming favour ascending UTI; fimbriae, biofilm, haemolysins, proteases and LPS. Diseases: UTIs (with stones), wound infections, sepsis. Proteus is naturally resistant to colistin and tetracyclines (and nitrofurantoin).

Note: one slide lists Proteus as spore-forming and glucose-negative; like all Enterobacteriaceae, Proteus does not form spores and ferments glucose.

The bacterial chromosome is a single, long, circular double-stranded DNA (1.5 to over 10 Mb depending on species), in the nucleoid attached to the membrane. It carries the structural genes for survival, growth, reproduction and regulation, and mobile elements (transposons, integrons, prophages, insertion sequences); it can lose or gain genes that confer resistance or virulence.

Plasmids are small (1-100 kb), stable, extrachromosomal dsDNA with independent replication, not essential for growth but carrying useful genes: resistance, metabolic, virulence, bacteriocin and pollutant-resistance plasmids. Conjugative plasmids carry tra genes and transfer themselves (e.g. the F plasmid of E. coli); non-conjugative plasmids can be mobilised with the help of a conjugative one. Plasmids are also vehicles for recombinant DNA technology.

Transposons ('jumping genes') change position within the genome, moving between chromosome and plasmids by recombination; they carry transposition genes and often resistance genes, and cannot replicate on their own. Integrons are bacterial systems that capture, express and disseminate genes in the form of cassettes, using an integrase; they sit on chromosomes, plasmids or transposons. Cassettes are inserted or excised by the integrase and, unlike transposons, do not code for the enzyme that moves them; many carry antibiotic resistance.

Phenotypic variation changes gene expression (regulation) in response to the environment: induced, reversible, not inherited, no change in the genome. Genotypic variation changes the genetic material by mutation or gene transfer, and is inherited.

A mutation is a sudden, spontaneous or induced, inherited change in a nucleotide sequence. Properties: stability (inherited, reversion rare), rarity (about 10⁻⁹ per nucleotide per generation), specificity (one trait at a time, which is why combination therapy, as in tuberculosis, reduces resistance) and spontaneity (random). Antibiotics do not induce resistance mutations: they select pre-existing resistant mutants, which then take over the population.

Bacteria exchange genes horizontally by three mechanisms. Transformation: uptake of naked DNA by competent bacteria (S. pneumoniae, Neisseria, H. influenzae). Griffith (1928) showed that harmless rough (R) pneumococci became virulent smooth (S), capsulated bacteria after mixing with heat-killed S bacteria: the 'transforming principle', later shown to be DNA. The same principle underlies cloning, e.g. insulin produced by bacteria.

Transduction: a bacteriophage (a virus of bacteria) carries a fragment of donor DNA to a recipient cell; phages are also being tested as therapy. Conjugation: transfer, usually of a plasmid, through cell-to-cell contact via a sex pilus, the commonest route in nature, within or between species; it spreads resistance and toxin genes. F+ cells carry the fertility plasmid, F− do not, and Hfr cells have integrated it into their chromosome.

Haemophilus ('blood-loving'), family Pasteurellaceae, 13 species (9 in humans). With Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella and Kingella it forms the HACEK group of oropharyngeal commensals that can cause infective endocarditis.

H. influenzae: small, pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacilli (0.3-1 µm), non-motile, non-sporing; oxidase, catalase and nitrate reductase positive; facultatively anaerobic, capnophilic; an obligate parasite of the human respiratory tract, spread by droplets. Strains are capsulated (six serotypes a-f; type b is the most virulent) or non-capsulated ('non-typeable'). It is fastidious: it needs X factor (haemin) and V factor (NAD), so it grows on chocolate agar but not on plain blood agar.

Three major surface antigens: the capsular polysaccharide, outer membrane proteins and lipopolysaccharide / lipo-oligosaccharide. The Hib capsule, polyribosyl-ribitol phosphate (PRP), is antiphagocytic and resists complement, allowing bloodstream invasion. Pili/fimbriae attach to the nasopharyngeal mucosa, IgA protease destroys mucosal IgA, OMPs and LPS aid adhesion and invasion, and LOS (endotoxin) drives inflammation.

Steps: colonisation of the nasopharynx (often silent) → local immune evasion (IgA protease) → invasion of the epithelium → bacteraemia, protected by PRP → haematogenous spread to meninges, epiglottis, lungs, joints → inflammation and tissue damage.

Encapsulated, mainly Hib (rarely types a, d, e, f): invasive disease, mostly in children aged 6 months to 2 years: meningitis, epiglottitis (sudden drooling, stridor, fever; airway emergency), septicaemia, septic arthritis, severe pneumonia, cellulitis. A vaccine exists.

Non-typeable strains (commensals of the upper airway): non-invasive infections in children and adults: otitis media, sinusitis, bronchitis, COPD exacerbations, conjunctivitis. No vaccine.

Diagnosis is direct only; there is no serological diagnosis (anti-Hib antibodies are measured only to check immunity in a vaccinated person). Samples: blood, CSF, sputum, throat swab, pus, joint, ear or sinus aspirates; never refrigerated (sensitive to cold and drying), transported at room temperature in gelled medium within 3 hours. Gram stain: pink pleomorphic coccobacilli. Culture: chocolate agar (heating lyses red cells, releasing X and V and inactivating NADases), 35-37 °C, 5-10% CO₂, 18-24 h; mucoid, convex, grey colonies. Satellitism: on blood agar, colonies grow around haemolytic S. aureus, which supplies V factor. Tests: X and V requirement, no haemolysis, indole and urease positive. Latex agglutination for capsular antigen b, MALDI-TOF, PCR.

Meningitis, epiglottitis, bacteraemia: IV ceftriaxone or cefotaxime (ampicillin if susceptible), with ICU airway care in epiglottitis. About 5% of isolates in the lecture produce a β-lactamase (penicillinase) and resist ampicillin/amoxicillin; otitis and sinusitis are then treated with amoxicillin-clavulanate or cefuroxime. Fluoroquinolones in adults only; tetracyclines avoided in children under 8 and in pregnancy. Rifampicin is the chemoprophylaxis for household or daycare contacts, especially with children under 4.

Vaccine: plain PRP is poorly immunogenic under 2 years, so it is conjugated to a protein carrier (tetanus or diphtheria toxoid, or an outer membrane protein: PRP-OMP). Primary doses at 2 and 4 (and 6) months with a booster at 11-15 months; universal vaccination cut childhood Hib meningitis by about 95%.

Note: a slide describes chocolate agar as 'heat-induced WBC lysis'; it is the red blood cells that are lysed to release X and V factors.

Saprophytism: environmental bacteria living on dead organic matter, usually harmless but opportunistic when host defences fail (Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter). Mutualism: both partners benefit (lactobacilli of the urogenital tract, Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron in the gut contribute to metabolism and protection). Commensalism: the bacterium benefits, the host is neither harmed nor helped (S. epidermidis, conjunctival flora, Proteus mirabilis). Parasitism: the bacterium benefits at the host's expense, causing tissue damage and disease (M. tuberculosis, Salmonella, Listeria).

Resident flora: fixed, generally non-pathogenic bacteria in deeper skin layers, re-establishing after disturbance and not washed off (Propionibacterium acnes). Transient flora: superficial, present for hours to weeks, removable by washing and often involved in transmission (S. aureus). Flora varies with age, diet, genetics and habitat. Internal organs and blood are sterile, and so is the fetus: the newborn acquires flora from its mother and environment. When resident flora is reduced (antibiotics) or the host is weakened (surgery, trauma, leukaemia, lymphoma, diabetes, cirrhosis), opportunists such as E. coli cause infection.

Pathogenicity is the ability to cause disease in a susceptible host (a quality: true pathogens such as Yersinia pestis, Bacillus anthracis). Virulence is the degree of pathogenicity, measured quantitatively, for example by the minimum infectious dose.

Virulence factors: (a) inhibition of phagocytosis: capsules (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae), preventing phagosome acidification (mycobacteria, Legionella), resisting lysosomal killing (Salmonella), killing the phagocyte with leucocidins or streptolysins (S. aureus, S. pyogenes), protein A blocking antibody Fc (staphylococci), M protein (streptococci); (b) adhesins: type 1 pili of E. coli on bladder epithelium, N. gonorrhoeae adhesins, streptococcal protein F binding fibronectin; (c) survival and intracellular growth: siderophores taking iron from lactoferrin and transferrin, IgA proteases (Neisseria, H. influenzae); (d) toxins; (e) extracellular enzymes: hyaluronidase, collagenase, coagulase, kinases, IgA proteases, leucocidins.

Three patterns of toxigenesis: toxin without colonisation (food poisoning), colonisation then toxin (cholera, diphtheria), colonisation then invasion (N. meningitidis). Exotoxins are highly toxic, specific proteins; treated with formalin they become toxoids, non-toxic but still antigenic: the basis of diphtheria and tetanus vaccines. Endotoxin is the lipopolysaccharide (lipid A) of Gram-negative outer membranes, released into tissues or blood; it binds LPS-binding protein, then CD14/TLR4/MD2 on monocytes, macrophages, dendritic and B cells, causing cytokine and TNF release, complement and coagulation activation (DIC) and septic shock.

Host receptivity depends on age, sex, nutrition, comorbidities, genetics and stresses (surgery, splenectomy, neutropenia, burns, corticosteroids, malnutrition). First line: physical (skin, mucus, mucociliary clearance, urination), chemical (acid pH of skin 4.7-5.7, stomach 1.5-3, vagina 3.8-5; lysozyme, defensins, IgA) and biological (microbiome). Second line: phagocytes, NK cells, complement, interferons, fever, inflammation. Third line: specific antibodies and T cells. Vaccines: toxoids (diphtheria, tetanus), killed bacteria (whole-cell pertussis), live attenuated (BCG), purified antigens (meningococcus, pneumococcus, acellular pertussis).

Nosocomial (healthcare-associated) infections appear after 48 h in hospital, affect 5-10% of inpatients and follow invasive procedures, the hospital environment and poor hygiene (UTIs, surgical sites, respiratory, catheter infections); community-acquired infections appear before 48 h. Infections are endogenous (own flora) or exogenous; some pathogens have humans as sole reservoir and healthy carriers (S. Typhi, meningococcus). Transmission is vertical or horizontal: contact (direct, indirect, droplet), vehicle (air, water, food, blood) or vector. Diseases are endemic, epidemic or pandemic.

Mycobacteria (family Mycobacteriaceae, order Actinomycetales) include M. tuberculosis, M. bovis, M. africanum, M. leprae (not cultivable) and atypical species (M. avium, M. kansasii, M. ulcerans) causing opportunistic mycobacterioses. Their lipid-rich wall resists decolourisation by acid and alcohol: they are acid-fast bacilli (AFB).

M. tuberculosis: slender, slightly curved rods (0.2-0.6 × 1-10 µm), non-motile, non-sporing, catalase and nitrate reductase positive, a strictly human pathogen with airborne transmission, a strict aerobe growing very slowly on Löwenstein-Jensen medium (colonies after up to 6 weeks at 37 °C). It is killed by UV light and sunlight, alcohol and bleach.

Tuberculosis remains a public health priority in Morocco: 29,018 new cases in 2020; between 2000 and 2023 incidence fell by about 19% and mortality by 6%. Risk factors: malnutrition, immunodepression (the HIV-TB association), and close contact with a contagious patient (family, health professionals).

About 10 inhaled bacilli reaching an alveolus can start infection. Alveolar macrophages ingest them, but mycobacteria block phagosome acidification and multiply inside. T-cell immunity forms a granuloma that contains them: latent infection. Outcomes: clearance, latent infection, primary progressive disease, or reactivation later when immunity falls; in the lecture about 60% of disease is pulmonary and 40% extrapulmonary. Surface lipids phthiocerol dimycocerosate (PDIM) and phenolic glycolipids (PGL) are major virulence factors.

Direct: microscopy, culture, nucleic acid tests, antigen detection. Indirect: tuberculin skin test, interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA), serology (not recommended). Samples: for lung disease, early-morning fasting sputum, bronchial or gastric aspirates, three times; for extrapulmonary disease, urine, CSF, pleural fluid, biopsies.

Microscopy: Ziehl-Neelsen (red bacilli on blue) or auramine fluorescence (faster screening). Culture: Löwenstein-Jensen, rough, dry, buff 'cauliflower' colonies in 2-6 weeks; liquid culture (MGIT) is faster. Classical tests: niacin positive, nitrate reduction positive, TCH resistant (unlike M. bovis). Current standard: PCR / NAAT such as GeneXpert, which also detects rifampicin resistance, and line probe assays.

Susceptibility testing for at least isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol should always be done. First-line drugs: rifampicin (R), isoniazid (H), pyrazinamide (Z), ethambutol (E) (and streptomycin). Standard drug-susceptible regimen: 6 months, 2RHZE / 4RH: an intensive phase of 2 months with four drugs, then 4 months of rifampicin + isoniazid. Directly observed therapy and a sputum check at 2 months. Extrapulmonary TB 6-9 months (up to 12 if severe); relapses need longer regimens; MDR/RR-TB ≥ 15 months with second-line drugs (amikacin, kanamycin, fluoroquinolones, cycloserine). Combinations prevent the selection of resistant mutants.

Prevention: finding and treating patients, screening family and contacts, and BCG at birth in the national immunisation plan.

Note: a slide lists mycobacteria among microaerophiles in the structure lecture; M. tuberculosis is a strict aerobe, as this lecture states.

Mycoplasmas belong to the class Mollicutes (Latin mollis, soft; cutis, skin), defined by the absence of a rigid cell wall. They are coccoid or filamentous and pleomorphic, do not fit the Gram classification, and are the smallest prokaryotes capable of autonomous multiplication (0.3-0.85 µm). Their membrane contains sterols (cholesterol) taken from the host, so they are fragile outside it. Non-motile, non-sporing, facultatively anaerobic; they grow at 37 °C, pH 7.4-7.8, in reduced oxygen with CO₂, on special rich media (SP-4, PPLO, modified Hayflick), and are frequent contaminants of cell cultures.

Species: M. pneumoniae, a strict human respiratory pathogen; M. genitalium, M. hominis and Ureaplasma urealyticum, urogenital colonisers and opportunists. Transmission: droplets, sexual contact, vertical.

Mycoplasmas are host-dependent, colonise mucosal surfaces and stay extracellular but tightly adherent to epithelium, often as asymptomatic colonisers. Virulence factors: an attachment (cytadherence) organelle with adhesins, variable surface proteins (antigenic variation), the CARDS toxin (ADP-ribosylating; inflammation and ciliary damage), hydrogen peroxide production and biofilm formation.

M. pneumoniae: tracheobronchitis, sore throat, ear inflammation and atypical ('walking') pneumonia; the lecture ranks it the second cause of community-acquired pneumonia after pneumococcus (the Chlamydia lecture ranks C. pneumoniae third). It can induce cold agglutinins (autoantibodies against red cells) and occasional systemic complications. M. hominis: pelvic inflammatory disease, pyelonephritis, spontaneous abortion, postpartum fever. Ureaplasma urealyticum: non-gonococcal urethritis in men, PID.

Direct: PCR is the gold standard on throat swabs or nasopharyngeal aspirates (no transport medium needed); rapid real-time platforms give results in about 4 hours. Culture is rarely done: slow (6-20 days for M. pneumoniae), needs enriched sterol media, CO₂, expertise, and is easily overgrown by contaminants. Indirect: serology (ELISA IgM, IgG, IgA; complement fixation; agglutination) on paired sera 2-4 weeks apart; IgM suggests recent infection; limits: delayed positivity, cross-reactions, poor value in immunocompromised patients.

Natural resistance to β-lactams and all drugs acting on peptidoglycan synthesis (no wall). Effective: macrolides and related MLSK drugs, tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones. Macrolides are usual in children (tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones are avoided); macrolide resistance has emerged in some regions.

Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) is a Gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococcus (sometimes short chains), 0.5-1.25 µm, a commensal of the upper respiratory tract transmitted by droplets. It has a polysaccharide capsule, its main virulence factor, defining over 90 serotypes (capsular typing with specific antisera: the Quellung / Neufeld reaction). It is catalase and oxidase negative, facultatively anaerobic, grows on enriched media (blood agar, chocolate agar) with 5-10% CO₂, giving α-haemolytic colonies that are round, shiny, mucoid when capsulated, with a concave ('draughtsman') centre from autolysis.

The cell wall carries the C polysaccharide, which reacts with human C-reactive protein (CRP was named after this reaction; CRP rises in inflammation and infection).

The capsule prevents binding of complement C3b, so bacteria escape phagocytosis unless type-specific antibodies are present. Pneumolysin (cytotoxin) lyses host cells, damages tissue and activates complement and inflammation. Autolysin (LytA) lyses the bacterium, releasing pneumolysin and wall fragments (and explaining bile solubility). PspA and PspC inhibit complement and help adherence; teichoic and lipoteichoic acids promote adherence and inflammation; neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid (colonisation); hyaluronidase helps spread; IgA1 protease cleaves secretory IgA.

Pneumococci usually sit asymptomatically in the nasopharynx; disease follows a viral infection or immune weakness. Diseases: pneumonia (the commonest cause of community-acquired pneumonia), otitis media, sinusitis (common under 3 years), bacteraemia and sepsis, and meningitis. Risk is highest at the extremes of age and after splenectomy.

Specimens: sputum, pleural fluid (thoracentesis), blood, CSF. Gram stain: Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci. Culture: blood or chocolate agar, 37 °C, CO₂; α-haemolytic mucoid colonies. Identification: catalase negative, optochin sensitive and bile soluble (sodium deoxycholate 2-10%), which separate it from viridans streptococci. Antigen detection: immunochromatographic tests (e.g. BinaxNOW) detect the C polysaccharide in urine or respiratory samples and stay positive after antibiotics. Molecular: PCR for lytA, ply and cps genes in blood, CSF or sputum, qPCR and LAMP; useful when cultures are negative.

Mild community pneumonia, otitis, sinusitis: amoxicillin (macrolide if allergic). Severe pneumonia or bacteraemia: IV penicillin G or ampicillin if susceptible, otherwise ceftriaxone or cefotaxime. Meningitis: high-dose IV ceftriaxone or cefotaxime + vancomycin until susceptibility is known. Penicillin-resistant strains (altered PBPs): third-generation cephalosporins or respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) in adults. Supportive care: oxygen, fluids, monitoring for sepsis.

Prevention: the conjugate vaccine, capsular polysaccharides linked to a carrier protein (a diphtheria protein), covering 13 serotypes in the lecture; Morocco's national programme gives three doses from 2 months of age. Conjugation turns the T-independent polysaccharide into a T-dependent antigen that works in infants.

About 50 Streptococcus species, commensal and pathogenic, are Gram-positive, catalase-negative cocci in chains or pairs. Lancefield grouping uses the cell wall carbohydrate antigen: A = S. pyogenes (pharyngitis, scarlet fever, skin infections, necrotising fasciitis, toxic shock); B = S. agalactiae (neonatal sepsis and meningitis); C and G (pharyngitis, skin, zoonoses); D = enterococci and S. bovis (endocarditis, UTI); F/G/L = S. anginosus group (abscesses).

Haemolysis on blood agar: β = complete lysis, a clear zone (S. pyogenes, S. agalactiae, S. aureus); α = partial, green, from hydrogen peroxide oxidising haemoglobin (S. pneumoniae); γ = none (Enterococcus faecalis).

S. pyogenes: Gram-positive cocci in chains (0.6-1 µm), non-motile, non-sporing, some capsulated (hyaluronic acid); aerobic and facultatively anaerobic; fastidious (blood-enriched media, 37 °C, CO₂). Small translucent colonies with a wide clear β-haemolysis zone. Habitat: throat and skin.

Key tests: catalase negative (vs staphylococci); bacitracin sensitive (vs other β-haemolytic streptococci); PYR positive (pyrrolidonyl peptidase; also positive in enterococci); Lancefield group A; CAMP negative and hippurate negative (vs group B); no growth in 6.5% NaCl and bile-aesculin negative (vs enterococci); bile insoluble (vs pneumococcus). Rapid antigen tests on throat swabs detect the group A carbohydrate: a positive result allows immediate treatment; a negative one in high suspicion needs a throat culture. PCR, qPCR and emm typing (M protein gene) serve research and epidemiology. ASO and anti-DNase B antibodies show a recent infection.

The membrane carries antigens resembling heart muscle, valve fibroblasts, skeletal and smooth muscle and neurons: molecular mimicry underlies autoimmune sequelae. Surface factors: M protein (antiphagocytic, the main virulence factor, basis of emm typing), protein F (binds fibronectin), lipoteichoic acid, hyaluronic acid capsule, C5a peptidase, streptococcal inhibitor of complement. Secreted: streptolysins O and S (haemolysins, kill phagocytes), streptokinase (dissolves clots), DNases, hyaluronidase, SpeB protease and superantigen toxins (streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins SpeA, SpeC and others) that activate T cells non-specifically: a cytokine storm in toxic shock, the rash of scarlet fever (erythrogenic toxins).

Pharyngitis, the most common: sore throat, fever, tonsillar exudate, tender cervical nodes; 5-15% of people are asymptomatic carriers. Scarlet fever: sandpaper rash spreading from the chest, strawberry tongue, fever. Skin: impetigo, erysipelas, cellulitis, lymphadenitis. Invasive: necrotising fasciitis (rapid destruction of fascia, severe pain, toxicity), streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, puerperal sepsis, bacteraemia, endocarditis.

Non-suppurative sequelae: acute rheumatic fever after untreated pharyngitis (fever, migratory polyarthritis, carditis, chorea; molecular mimicry) and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis after pharyngitis or impetigo (haematuria, oedema, hypertension; immune complexes in glomeruli).

Penicillin (V oral, G IV/IM) is the drug of choice: no resistance reported; amoxicillin in children. Penicillin allergy: macrolides (resistance by mef efflux pumps) or clindamycin. Pharyngitis: 10 days of treatment to prevent rheumatic fever; skin infections 7-10 days. Severe invasive disease (necrotising fasciitis, toxic shock): IV penicillin + clindamycin (clindamycin stops toxin synthesis) with surgery and supportive care. Prevention: isolation, early treatment of the acute phase and of relapses.

Note: one slide says PYR activity is typical of all streptococci; in practice PYR is positive in group A streptococci and enterococci and negative in most other streptococci, which is what makes it useful.

Microbiology studies microscopic organisms: bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites. Bacteria matter because their structure and physiology explain mechanisms of infection (adhesion, invasion, toxins, immune evasion), diagnosis, antibiotic choice and resistance, and prevention. Bacteria are autonomous single cells with DNA, feeding from their environment and treated with antibiotics; viruses have DNA or RNA, need a host cell to replicate and do not respond to antibiotics.

The light microscope (40-1000×, with Gram, Ziehl-Neelsen or Giemsa stains) shows shape, arrangement, capsules and spores (bacteria are about 1 µm). Electron microscopy resolves 5-10 nm: SEM for surfaces (pili, biofilm), TEM for internal structures; mostly research use.

Prokaryotes are 0.2-5 µm, divide by binary fission, have no nuclear membrane (a nucleoid), no membrane-bound organelles, 70S ribosomes (80S in eukaryotes), a single circular chromosome without histones, a membrane generally without sterols, and a peptidoglycan cell wall. Components: external appendages (flagella, pili, fimbriae), glycocalyx (capsule, slime), envelope (outer membrane in Gram-negatives, peptidoglycan, cell membrane) and internal parts (cytoplasm, ribosomes, inclusions, nucleoid, sometimes endospores).

Genetic material: the chromosome carries essential genes; plasmids are small non-essential DNA molecules that may carry resistance or virulence genes. Glycocalyx: a thick rigid capsule (K. pneumoniae, Haemophilus, S. pneumoniae, B. anthracis) protects from phagocytosis, defines serotypes (over 100 for pneumococcus) and is the basis of vaccines (Hib, pneumococcus); a thinner slime layer allows attachment and biofilm (S. mutans).

Gram-positive walls have a thick peptidoglycan with teichoic and lipoteichoic acids; Gram-negative walls a thin peptidoglycan, a periplasmic space and an outer membrane with lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin) and porins. Peptidoglycan is chains of N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid cross-linked by peptides; β-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), block its synthesis and the cell bursts from internal pressure. The Gram stain exploits these differences: positives stay purple, negatives turn pink.

The cytoplasmic membrane controls selective transport, secretes enzymes, carries receptors for chemotaxis, houses enzymes for DNA, wall and lipid synthesis and the respiratory chain. Flagella give motility and carry H antigens used for identification; arrangements: monotrichous, lophotrichous, amphitrichous, peritrichous. Fimbriae: short, numerous, for adhesion and biofilm. Pili: longer, few; sex (conjugation) pili transfer plasmids. Endospores (Bacillus, Clostridium) resist heat, drying and starvation and germinate when conditions improve. Shapes: cocci (pairs, chains, clusters), bacilli, curved and spiral forms.

Physical: temperature (psychrophiles, psychrotrophs that spoil refrigerated food such as Pseudomonas, mesophiles 10-47 °C including most pathogens, thermophiles, hyperthermophiles), pH (most at 6.5-7.5), water and osmotic pressure (halophiles need salt; osmotolerant bacteria such as staphylococci tolerate it). Chemical: oxygen: obligate aerobes (Pseudomonas, Neisseria), obligate anaerobes (Clostridium, Bacteroides), facultative anaerobes (E. coli, staphylococci), aerotolerant anaerobes and microaerophiles (Campylobacter). Oxygen tolerance depends on superoxide dismutase and catalase/peroxidase, which strict anaerobes lack. Carbon (autotrophs use CO₂; heterotrophs, including pathogens, use organic compounds), nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus, trace elements and growth factors for auxotrophs (e.g. Haemophilus).

Culture media are sterile (autoclave, 120 °C). By state: solid (1.5-2% agar, colonies), semi-solid (≤ 0.5%, motility, transport), liquid (broth, turbidity; blood cultures). By use: simple (nutrient agar), enriched (blood agar, chocolate agar), selective (MacConkey for Gram-negatives, mannitol salt for staphylococci), enrichment (selenite F for Salmonella), differential (lactose on MacConkey, mannitol on Chapman, haemolysis on blood agar), transport (Cary-Blair, Amies).

Bacteria divide by binary fission. In a closed culture the growth curve has four phases: lag (adaptation, no increase), exponential (log) (fastest division), stationary (division equals death) and death. A colony is the product of 20-30 divisions of one bacterium.

Metabolism = catabolism (breaking molecules down, releasing energy) + anabolism (building molecules, consuming energy), coupled by ATP. Aerobic respiration uses O₂ as final electron acceptor (up to 38 ATP per glucose); anaerobic respiration uses another inorganic acceptor such as nitrate; fermentation uses an organic acceptor and yields only 2 ATP (alcoholic, lactic in streptococci and lactobacilli, mixed acids in enterobacteria).

Note: one slide lists mycobacteria among microaerophiles. M. tuberculosis is an obligate aerobe, which is why it favours the well-oxygenated lung apices.
